newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe calls parliament confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe calls parliament confidence vote.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, seeking to unite a fractious centre-right coalition, said on Tuesday he would seek a vote of confidence in his economic policy when parliament reconvenes next week after the summer recess.

"To renew the contract that unites us for this legislative period, especially in the eyes of the French public, I will seek a confidence vote in the National Assembly after a policy statement at the start of the new session," Juppe told lawmakers of the Union for French Democracy (UDF) junior coalition party.
The session begins next Tuesday. Since the coalition holds four-fifths of the seats in the 577-member assembly, the outcome of the vote is a foregone conclusion.

However Juppe's tactic appeared aimed at outflanking critics of austerity in his own ranks, led by former Gaullist interior minister Charles Pasqua, a leading opponent of a single European currency, and outspoken UDF free-marketeer Alain Madelin.

Several coalition politicians have criticised his planned income tax cuts as inadequate and sought a change in economic priorities to boost sluggish growth and combat record 12.5 percent unemployment.
By calling a confidence motion, Juppe is effectively challenging his critics to put up or shut up.
"Our mortal enemy is division and dissent...The antidote to division and dissent is unity," he declared.
But the prime minister, often criticised as authoritarian, injected a conciliatory note in his speech to UDF legislators.

"The government is listening to its (parliamentary) majority. The debate on bills which we are going to put to you, especially the draft budget, is meant to enable improvements, even shifts in directon. I am open to that as I have always said," he said.
The confidence debate comes as Juppe and President Jacques Chirac have slumped back close to the record unpopularity they reached during last year's labour unrest.
An opinion poll published on Sunday showed public approval of Chirac had fallen by seven points to 31 percent in September and Juppe's rating stood at a mere 27 percent, down four points.
Socialist opposition floor leader Laurent Fabius compared Juppe's government to the orchestra continuing to play aboard the Titanic as the cruise liner hit an iceberg and sank.
"The country's economic situation is calamitous. It's easy to understand why the French people are gloomy," Fabius told Socialist parliamentarians meeting in Figeac.
"Regardless of the economic and social results, the government orchestra goes on playing on the Titanic," he said.
Juppe defended his economic policies, dismissed talk of a recession prompted by a recent slowdown and stressed he would stick to the goal of European monetary union.

"To give up now when we are so close to the goal would not only be regrettable, pathetic. It would be an error with heavy consequences, wasting the efforts made by the entire nation for several years, by our companies and our citizens," he said.
Juppe sought to cheer UDF deputies by promising to bring forward a bill this autumn to fight the use of illegal labour, a problem widely associated with illegal immigration.

But he drew some jeers when he mentioned his idea of introducing a dose of proportional representation for 1998 parliamentary elections, prompting him to snap back that several UDF members had made similar requests to him.
